criterion_notes.c1: Examines household piped drinking-water service access, specifically service availability/continuity (interruptions of at least one full day in the past fortnight) in urban and peri-urban Zambia.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type mechanism governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) is examined: DHS home ownership (labelled tenure in S13 Table) is included solely as a household socio-economic/coping proxy (capacity to buy a storage tank) among households already using piped water; NWASCO regulator and IBNET utility datasets contribute only aggregate operational supply metrics (hours/day, LPCD, and non-revenue water percentage); and all 11 providers are commercial Water and Sewerage Companies entered only as unanalysed provider dummy variables alongside regional GDP per capita. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the study also fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because regulator and utility data are used as monitoring data streams measuring water supply availability/loss rather than testing a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor, even though surface terminology mentions regulator reports, service providers, non-revenue water, and home ownership.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative cross-sectional study integrating georeferenced 2018 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey data (n = 3,047 households in 177 clusters) with 2017 IBNET utility records and 2018 NWASCO regulator reports using bivariate tests and two-level logistic regression.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports user-reported piped drinking-water availability/intermittency (water unavailable from the main piped source for at least one full day in the preceding two weeks), compared against regulator- and utility-reported service continuity (hours/day) and quantity supplied (LPCD).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (3,047 urban and peri-urban piped-water-using households nested in 177 DHS clusters across 11 WSC coverage areas in Zambia), household/cluster/provider explanatory variables, binary interruption outcome, and cross-sectional multilevel study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The primary objective of this study was therefore to assess the added value of utility and regulator data in estimating piped water availability and quantifying risk factors for piped water intermittency and related inequalities.
Household ‘user’ data from the 2018 Demographic and Health Survey (n = 3047) were spatially linked to provider data from an international utility database and regulator reports.
To assess drinking-water availability, participating households are asked ‘In the last two weeks, was the water from your main source not available for at least one full day?’.

The annual average duration of water service (hours/day) at the customer connection, and the average amount of water consumed in LPCD were extracted from the publicly available 2018 NWASCO report [42] for each WSC.
Home ownership relates to the choice of water service and ability to cope with piped water interruptions.
Provider and regulator availability–reported average service hours expressed as hrs/day and LCPCD were used and treated as continuous variables.

raw_response.exposure: Household socio-economic and seasonal factors (native language, month/season of interview, type of piped service, household wealth, household size, home ownership), DHS cluster factors (neighbourhood wealth, degree and change of urbanisation, maximum length of residency), and provider-level operational/economic factors (GDP per capita at service provider level, non-revenue water percentage, regulator/provider reported hours/day and LPCD, and WSC provider dummy variables)
raw_response.outcome: User-reported piped drinking-water interruption of at least one full day in the two weeks prior to survey (binary), alongside regulator- and provider-reported service continuity (hrs/day) and consumption (LPCD)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 3,047 urban and peri-urban households using piped drinking-water nested within 177 clusters from the 2018 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey across 11 commercial Water and Sewerage Company (WSC) coverage areas in Zambia
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the study empirically examines piped drinking-water intermittency in urban and peri-urban Zambia using linked DHS household survey, IBNET utility, and NWASCO regulator datasets, it does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water service access. Regulator and utility reports are used strictly as monitoring data sources supplying operational availability and water-loss metrics (service hours/day, LPCD, and non-revenue water percentage), provider variation across the 11 commercial utilities is modelled only via unanalysed dummy variables and regional GDP per capita, and household home ownership is included solely as a socio-economic proxy for household coping capacity among existing piped-water users rather than a tenure or documentation requirement.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional spatial data-linkage and two-level logistic regression analysis of secondary household survey, utility, and regulator data
